text: TUESDAY, MAY 11, 1926.

label: text
text: There are many thinking people in South Africa who are alarmed at the colour segregation policy of the present Government. These people have found an outspoken champion of their thoughts in the Bishop of Pretoria, Dr. Talbot, who has not only attacked the native and Asiatic policy of the Government, but has now shown many of the dangers and the fallacies that He hidden in the Colour Bar Bill. It would seem that this bill limiting the labour activities of the native, will shortly be on the Statute-book of Me. Union. A solemn "warning of the probable consequences has been written by the Bishop of Pretoria in the March issue of "Kingdom," the official organ of his diocese.

label: text
text: Beginning with the argument that Christianity stands or falls by its assertion of the equal value of all souls before God, Dr. Talbot goes on:—

label: text
text: At present the great mass of native life is at a lower level of human attainment than the European. Not that we can say that the native is inherently inferior to the European. Evidence from America of what has been attained by the negro suggests that he is not inherently inferior, but that he is in the main at a lower level of development compared with the European. It would be sheer sentimentality to deny this.

label: text
text:
Predilection for Cheap Labour.
And yet this conclusion does not mitigate my deep-sealed dismay at the trend of present South African legislation at the expense of the native. I cannot think that the need to protect the white worker from being swamped by native labour justifies the introduction of the principle of the colour bar into the law of the land. I do not disregard unsympathetically the anxiety of white labour lest it be swamped, for, after all, it is working with a partner—namely, capital—that has evinced again and again as terrible predilection for cheap labour. I noticed that the President of the Chamber of Mines in a recent public speech had little more to contribute to the discussion of the problems of South African industry than the contention that the one thing to do was to import and to keep on importing as much cheap native labour to the mines as possible. But I do believe that the protection of the white worker should be secured by custom, by negotiation and regulation within industry, and not by legislation.

label: text
text: The passing of the bill of the Assembly is an evil omen for the future. Even though it is leniently and gently administered it cannot but engender a sense in the intelligent native's mind that the white man means to keep the black man down. It is not only a question of its actual provisions nor its administration, but its symbolic character. It will symbolise the inherent inferiority of the native and the resolve to use him only as a means to white convenience. It will hang in front of native hope and aspiration that which suppresses, confines, and excludes. I think it is a blind and essentially tyrannical measure, and if it is finally ratified it will have inevitably disastrous results to the true peace and wealth of South Africa. It makes it worse that the bill includes Indians with natives. In its scope, for the argument about actual inferiority is not nearly so strong in regard to the Indian as in regard to the Bantu. There are in India, and there may well be in South Africa, Indians who though of dark skin are on a level with the finest flower of European culture. That an able gifted son of India should be debarred on the ground of colour from rising to his fullest development and capacity is a great wrong; and it brings out into added relief the injustice done to the Bantu people.

label: text
text:
Encourage Native Progress.
Surely this legislation is in the wrong direction—namely, that of discouraging native growth. The right direction is that of encouraging native progress. If the black men can rise to the level of capacity with the white men, then it should be the endeavour of the white men not to keep them out but to bring them in at the white level of conditions and reward. This would entail the surmounting of great difficulties. It would be no short cut to this end, it would be no solution of the native problem. There is no short cut, there is no solution. There is no short cut through this whole business.

SHANGHAI WANTS NEW BUILDING
The American Consulate-General announces that Consul General Cunningham has received from Congressman Dyer a telegram stating that the Senate had passed the Foreign Service Buildings Act of 1928. It is believed that the Senate has passed the bill in practically the same form in which it was passed by the House on March 15, and if so the bill will become a law immediately upon signature by the President. The funds will be available after July 1.

label: text
text:
The bill carries an appropriation: of G.$10,000,000 to be allocated for foreign service buildings in the various parts of the world under the direction of the Foreign Service Buildings Commission, which is composed of the Secretary of State, the Secretary of the Treasury, the Secretary of Commerce, the Chairman and the Ranking Minority Member of the Committee on Foreign Relations of the Senate, and the Chairman and Ranking Minority Member of the Committee on Foreign Affairs of the House of Representatives.
The personnel of the Committee at the present time therefore will be Frank B. Kellogg, Andrew W. Mellon, Herbert Hoover, Senator William E. Borah of Idaho, Senator Claude A. Swanson of Virginia, Congressman Stephen G. Porter of Pennsylvania and Congressman J. Charles Linthicum of Maryland.
Consult General Cunningham believes that the next step which should be taken is to convince the Foreign Service Buildings Commission, of the importance of Shanghai and also of the amount which should be allocated for the construction of building here. He believes that there is a good chance of participating in the early allocation of the funds but it is essential that every American consider it his duty to make known to his friends in the United States the importance and the needs of this port.

label: text
text: One of the strongest arguments in favour of Shanghai is the large number of United States Government officials functioning here, the Department of State being represented by the Consulate-General and the United States Court for China; the Department of Commerce by the offices of the Trade Commissioner, Registrar of the China Trade Act and United States Shipping Board Representative; the Treasury Attache and the Public Health Service; and the United States Navy being represented ashore by the Navy. No doubt, some people will say to me, "Yes, but the Colour Bar Bill is part of the Prime Minister's general scheme of native policy. It is part of the policy of differential treatment—viz., working towards the development of native life in native reserves in the country and the securing of the fullest industrial opportunity for Europeans." Well, I think we must do our best to believe that, and I intend to do so. But the Colour Bar Bill is a wretched preliminary to the rest of the policy. It is no better than passing a harrowing area a cricket pitch before the match is begun.—"Manchester Guardian"

label: text
text: Commander Sir Graham Bower, R.N., K.C.M.G. (Ex-President of Grotius Society and Member of the Council of International Law Association), writing in "The Navy" says:

label: text
text: War between nations is a conflict of wills. It may be a commercial war, a war for the acquisition of territory, or a war in defence of an ally, but in every case it is a menna by which a nation seeks to coerce or resist the will of another nation. It is not merely a conflict of armies or navies, but a conflict of nations, and it is possible that the will of a nation may be coerced whilst its armies and navies are still undefeated. But in war between civilised nations it has been generally recognised that the methods of coercion shall be so limited that useless cruelty and useless suffering shall not be imposed. Montesquieu's dictum remains as true to day as when it was published more than a century and a half ago. In his "Esprit des Lois" he tells us that "The Law of Nations is naturally founded on this principle, that different nations ought, in time of peace, to do one another all the good they can, and, in time of war, as little injury as possible without prejudicing their real interests. The object of war is victory that of victory conquest, and that of conquest preservation. From this and the preceding principle all these rules are derived which constitute the Law of Nations."

label: text
text: War is cruel. It is as cruel to kill a soldier as it is to kill a child. But civilised nations recognise that because the killing of soldiers and sailors is necessary to victory it is legitimate, whilst the killing of non-combatants, women and children, is illegitimate because the death of non-combatants, women and children does not weaken the enemy's power of resistance. It inflicts useless and unprofitable suffering, and strengthens the national will to resist. From this root principle civilised nations have sought to establish a clear distinction between combatants and non-combatants in time of war.

label: text
text: The weapons of war have been improved and new weapons have been invented which have been more deadly or more effective means of coercion. The breech loading rifles and machine-gun's were more deadly and more effective than the spears of the Dervishes, but their use was legitimate so long as they were used against combatants and not against non-combatants. The submarine is a new weapon of war, an instrument for the coercion of the will of the enemy, and it follows that it is a legitimate weapon of war so long as it is used as a means of coercing an enemy nation and does not inflict unprofitable loss or suffering on non-combatants. There can be no objection to the legitimate use of the submarine. There is the strongest possible objection to its misuse. That the submarine was misused on many occasions in the great European war cannot be disputed; but it is also true that on many other occasions it was used, legitimately as weapon of war, in strict observance of the laws of war. Its main use was that of a commerce destroyer, but it was also used, and effectively used, both in the North Sea and at the Dardanelles, as weapon against warships, whilst the British submarine rendered valuable service in the Heligolan. Bight as the advanced outposts of the British Fleet and as commerce destroyers and fighting ships in the Baltic. It is not too much to say that Riga was saved by the torpedoing of the "Moltke" by a British submarine.

label: text
text: And since the war the submarine has been developed. In the early years of the war the submarine was a vessel of small size with a limited radius of action. Our latest submarine, the X1, is a vessel of 2,700 tons surface displacement and can circumnavigate the world.

label: text
text: The torpedo has been popularly regarded as the chief weapon of the submarine. That it is its most deadly weapon is true, but it is also true that it is not the weapon that has been most in use. For instance, during her cruise in the Mediterranean, in June, 1916, the German U36 sunk forty-one vessels, but out of this number only two were sunk by torpedo. The gun was the most economical and the favourite weapon of the submarine, and the torpedo was, as a rule, only used against a vessel known to be, or suspected of being armed.

label: text
text: During the war the German submarine proved efficient in two roles: as a weapon of coast defence, and as a commerce destroyer. No one disputes that the use of the submarine as a weapon of coast defence is legitimate and the only question open to discussion is: How far and under what

It is, however, obvious that she could not provide accommodation for the passengers and crew of an Atlantic liner, which may, and often doe carry a population of 3,000 souls. But neither could a destroyer or cruiser provide accommodation for such a population or even for the population of a much smaller mail steamer, and it is now generally acknowledged that to place the passengers and crew in the boats is not to provide adequately for their safety, more especially as there may be invalids or young children amongst them.
It is evident therefore that the declaration in the Fourth Article of the Washington Treaty needs amendment. So we come to this Should not the destruction of unarmed merchant ships be entirely prohibited to all vessels of war whether submarines or surface ships? For they are all equally incapable of providing suitable accommodation and the destruction of unarmed marchants ships, involving as it does cruelty and suffering to neutrals and non-combatants, it is not as means of coercing the will of an enemy and certainly not a legit climate means.
The solution of the problem is therefore to be found in the total prohibition of the destruction of unarmed and non-combatant prizes and the return to the former practice of requiring that prizes shall

And it is the more imperative to avoid invidious distinction between one class of war vessel and another inasmuch as the submarine is now recognised as one of the cheapest and most efficient modes of coast defence and also the weapon of the weaker Naval Power.

label: text
text: It would be impossible to land an army in England in the presence of a fleet of submarines. It would be equally impossible to land an army in the Philippines or Australia if the coasts and harbours were protected by submarines. The French rely on submarines to protect their communications with Algiers, and the Americans regard them as their best coastal defence, whilst the smaller States rely on them as their only protection against battle fleets. Germany has no submarines and is not allowed to build any England is still the strongest Naval Power in Europe and to propose the abolition of submarines would expose the British nation to the suspicion of selfish motives. But to prohibit the destruction of unarmed ships by war vessels of any type and to require that prizes shall be brought into port for adjudication is to ask that a law which was observed for centuries shall be once more enforced. The armed merchant ship is a fighting ship and must take her chance with other fighting ships. But the unarmed vessel is a non-combatant and is entitled to the exemption and the status of a non-combatant that status should be granted to her by both surface ships and submarines. In this manner will the protection for non-combatants and neutrals sought for by the Washington Conference be best attained.

label: text
text: It may be that to secure this an England and America would have to concede the right of asylum for enemy prizes in neutral ports, but the sacrifice is worth making. If not for selfish reason, then for the lake of humanity.

label: text
text: No fair-minded person desires to deprive a combatant of methods of coercion necessary for self-defence or for victory, but all humanity has the right to demand that these methods shall be used without injury or cruelty to neutrals and ion-combatants, and it is evident that the destruction of non-combatant ships cannot be carried out without such injury or cruelty.
